description.narrative: Our Voices Our Futures (OVOF) will use capacity-building and convenings among feminist movements to strengthen and build movements within countries and across regions, while also link feminist movements to relevant actors, such as internet rights’ movements, Dutch allies and progressive policymakers. OVOF believes in strengthening movements from within, to create more inclusive, powerful and resilient movements. To influence laws and policies at national and international levels, OVOF sees this as the only sustainable mitigation strategy in relation to the increasing power of anti-rights and anti-gender forces

UHAI-EASHRI has a target of two feminist organisations, women’s rights and sexual rights CSOs and movements with enhanced skills and capacity to influence legal and policy processes and integrate feminist and human rights perspectives into their advocacy.

Negative attitudes and perceptions towards Structurally Silenced Women in Kenya have created an environment where members of the public are increasingly against communities of sexual and gender minorities and sex workers and their rights. UHAI's Structurally Silenced Women-led partners prioritised strengthening partnerships with allies and Structurally Silenced Women's organisations instead as a way to progressively work towards greater engagement with mainstream Women's Rights organisations and feminist partners.

UHAI-EASHRI has a target of two feminist organisations, women’s rights and sexual rights CSOs and movements with enhanced skills and capacity to influence legal and policy processes and integrate feminist and human rights perspectives into their advocacy.

Representatives of four East African organisations attended the CEDAW Convening in Namibia. Their participation brought rich, firsthand perspectives on the lived realities of LBQT criminalisation and strategic litigation, including sharing critical insights on security risks and network instability. The Convening provided much-needed solidarity, and an opportunity to build a robust support network, ultimately enhancing their capacity to advocate effectively for their communities. UHAI partner participated to CREA’s SGRI earlier this year—a pivotal experience that enhanced their organizational capacity in gender rights, intersectionality, and sexuality. This global program enriched their approach to campaign development, ensuring that their advocacy is rooted in an inclusive and intersectional understanding of human rights. The insights and strategies gained were reported to have been directly integrated into their ongoing digital campaigns, amplifying the voices of queer individuals in Kenya and strengthening their global network with activists and organizations.UHAI partner organised human rights awareness sessions - these community-based forums focused on raising awareness of human rights, relevant legal frameworks, and practical strategies for self-protection. In addition to legal literacy, the sessions provided a safe space to discuss mental health concerns and highlighted the urgent need for specialized psychosocial support for survivors of gender-based violence (GBV). UHAI partner implemented three focused forums to address intersecting issues related to sexual and reproductive health (SRH), HIV stigma, and substance abuse among LBQGNC womxn in Western Kenya. Safe Use of Sex Toys and SRH Forum: participants received education on the safe use of sex toys, consent, and body autonomy, resulting in increased awareness of healthy sexual practices and a reduction in associated reproductive health risks. HIV Stigma and SRH Forum: this session focused on the detrimental effects of HIV-related stigma on the sexual and reproductive health of LBQGNC individuals. The forum fostered a supportive environment by enhancing participants’ understanding of stigma’s impact, paving the way for ongoing stigma reduction initiatives and more inclusive healthcare practices. Drug and Substance Abuse Training: Targeting LBQGNC womxn from diverse backgrounds, this training built capacity to address the risks of drug and substance abuse. Participants—comprising activists, community leaders, and healthcare providers—acquired practical strategies for prevention, intervention, and support, reinforcing community resilience and a proactive approach to substance abuse challenges.The implementation of these three focused forums has led to a measurable improvement in the overall well-being and empowerment of LBQGNC womxn in Western Kenya. Increased awareness of safe sexual practices has reduced reproductive health risks, while enhanced understanding of HIV stigma has paved the way for more inclusive healthcare services. Additionally, practical strategies for prevention and intervention in substance abuse have strengthened community resilience and empowered local leaders and activists to address these challenges proactively, ultimately fostering a safer and more supportive environment.UHAI partner conducted a series of empowerment meetings equipping female sex workers (FSWs) with practical knowledge of their legal rights through interactive sessions, including discussions and role-play exercises. These activities significantly boosted their confidence in asserting their rights and improved their ability to engage constructively with law enforcement and other stakeholders, fostering greater agency and protection in their daily lives. There is a recognised increase in the confidence and agency of female sex workers. These sessions have enhanced their ability to assert their rights and engage effectively with law enforcement and stakeholders. As a result, female sex workers now demonstrate greater resilience, improved access to legal and protection services.

comment.narrative: Structurally silenced women's organisations in Kenya need capacity strengthening to resource efforts to continuously build their movements anchored in political thought. Institutional and individual leadership development over time supports this.
At least 1 collective action/initiative of structurally silenced women, groups and organisations to promote structurally silenced women's inclusion and defend structurally silenced women's rights.

1) One day members forum to impart knowledge on needs and concerns that relates to sex workers human needs and rights. And created the space for sex workers to share their plights and issues, during this forum champions/representatives were chosen; to represent sex workers in the various hotspots that were mapped out by members. 2) Mapped out sex worker friendly healthcare facilities, organised and facilitated one day sensitisation meeting with healthcare workers; to sensitise them on issues of stigma and discrimination that sex workers face. The organisation also managed to conduct an awareness and sensitisation meeting for members. Sex workers were informed of their rights and were also sensitised on the different health care services available to them. 3) Convening of mental health activity, where they linked their members with the relevant stakeholders (certified counsellor) and shared their contact for interactions and counselling sessions at a subsidised fee. Trans*Sisters Network also managed to map out areas in their county of operation where security and wellbeing of their members can be compromised and coached their members on precautions to prevent violence prevalence, The partners deliberated on the importance of prioritising personal safety and shared a hotline number for emergency response. 4) Security training was conducted for 40 LBQ activists. 5) Held sessions with 71 LBQ constituents on burnout. 6) The Partners held a three-day capacity development strategy workshop, with INEND staff and Experiential leadership fellowship cohort partners. 7) Awareness among the service providers within Busia, on the needs of the transgender and gender non-conforming community and where they can be referred for the services. The partners mentioned in their report that they sensitized health care workers on transgender and gender non-conforming persons on comprehensive sexual and rproductive health. 8) Dialogue forums with Health Care Workers. The partners managed to sensitise the County Health Management Team in Busia. 9) Sensitisation and LBQ security response officers training.The partners were able to develop standard operating procedures and a reporting toolkit which was used to train 4 LBQ security response officers on how they would handle security violations meted against LBQ persons and how to enter cases into the reporting template. 10) Support to get security response team to address issues raised by LBQ women. 11-12) Conducted 2 stakeholder meetings focusing on different health departments, specific to SRHR, Mental health, and Covid-19. 13) A local partner organised a one day forum with key stakeholders such as police, boda-boda riders, bar owners, hotspot representatives, village elders and other stakeholders to create awareness on human rights and need of sex workers. The organisation managed to create an awareness and advocacy forum for the rights of sex workers and to mitigate violence against these groups.

CFCS VIII Pan-African Activists panel discussion: Focused on highlighting key elements of the dynamic socio-political context in East African countries such as Kenya where polarised public discourse on the rights LGBTIQ+ persons fueled negative attitudes towards UHAI’s sexual and gender minority communities. On the panel was representation of UHAI’s structurally silenced women and communities. Resourcing for under-funded and under-resourced movements such as LBQGNC, was discussed as an area that needed much more proactive attention from funders and allied partners. The need for being considerate of the dynamics within East African SSW/C movements. The activists centred wellness in the resilience building of our communities that continue to be adversely affected by the various forms of violence they face in all spaces.The activists shared priorities for SSC communities in Kenya which were around increased and sustained support towards nationa level coordination focused on safety and security and strategising for advocacy that pushes back against the anti-gender and anti-rights efforts manifesting as anti-LGBT legislation (re: Family Protection Bill, legislation banning public debate on LGBT issues)
